Space

A person should be able to walk outside, look up, and know what they are seeing; explain why things orbit instead of falling; say honestly how big and how old the universe is; know how we got off this planet; and tell a real result from a headline.

30 lessons at middle school level, taught at a kitchen table with everyone on their own screen. Each lesson is 45 minutes and is built around things you click, not things you watch.

Each lesson is one page you scroll through together. Arrow keys move a slide at a time. The Notes link in the corner of every lesson opens the teacher cue sheet — beat by beat, one line each. Open it on a phone.

0. Looking Up

Starts with a light in the sky they cannot name and ends with them knowing what they are looking at, which way it is moving, and how hopelessly far away it is.

  • 01
    What Is That Light?

    Look at anything in the night sky and say whether it is a star, a planet, a satellite, a plane or a meteor, and give the reason.

  • 02
    The Sky Turns

    Explain the night's motion and the year's changing constellations without saying that the stars move, and find north from the sky.

  • 03
    How Far Is Far?

    Build the solar system to scale, put the Sun, Pluto and the nearest star in proportion, and say what it means that everything they see is old light.

1. Gravity and Orbits

The one piece of physics the rest of the course leans on. Ends with them able to say why a satellite does not fall down and why an astronaut floats.

  • 04
    Everything Falls

    Predict which of two dropped objects lands first and why, and compute their own weight on any world from its mass and radius.

  • 05
    Falling and Missing

    Explain an orbit as falling sideways fast enough to miss, and say why low orbits are fast, high orbits are slow, and escape is neither.

  • 06
    Why Astronauts Float

    Explain weightlessness without using the phrase 'no gravity', and say what is actually different inside a falling box.

  • 07
    Orbits Are Not Circles

    Draw an ellipse, say where an orbiting thing speeds up and why, and explain why a comet is only visible for a few weeks.

2. Sun, Earth, Moon

The three-body clockwork responsible for day, year, season, phase, eclipse and tide. Everything here is predictable from geometry.

  • 08
    Why There Are Seasons

    Kill the 'summer is closer to the Sun' idea with evidence, and predict day length and sun angle for any date and latitude.

  • 09
    The Moon's Phases

    Predict the Moon's phase from the Sun-Earth-Moon geometry, say what time it rises, and explain why we only ever see one side.

  • 10
    Eclipses and Tides

    Explain why there is not an eclipse every month, and why there are two high tides a day rather than one.

3. The Solar System

A tour with a thesis: distance from the Sun explains almost everything about what a world turned out to be.

  • 11
    The Sun Is the Whole Story

    State the Sun's share of the solar system's mass, describe fusion in a sentence, and connect a sunspot to an aurora.

  • 12
    Rock, Air and Greenhouse

    Compare the four rocky planets on four numbers and explain why Venus is hotter than Mercury.

  • 13
    Giants, Moons and Rings

    Say why the outer planets are big and gassy, why rings sit where they do, and why the missions go to moons rather than planets.

  • 14
    Rubble and Ice

    Use asteroid, meteor, meteorite and comet correctly, estimate an impact, and argue a side on whether Pluto is a planet.

4. Light and Stars

Light is the only thing that ever reaches us, so this unit is about reading it. Ends with them getting a star's temperature, ingredients and fate out of its colour.

  • 15
    Light Is the Only Messenger

    Order the spectrum by energy, say what each kind of telescope is for, and explain why a bigger mirror is a better one.

  • 16
    Reading a Star

    Get temperature from colour, ingredients from spectral lines, and motion from a shift, and separate brightness from luminosity.

  • 17
    How Stars Live

    Place a star on the H-R diagram from its colour and brightness, and predict its whole life from one number: its mass.

  • 18
    How Stars Die

    Say what a star of a given mass leaves behind, explain an event horizon without magic, and trace an atom in their own body to a star.

5. The Universe

Zooming out past the last thing with a name. Ends with an honest account of what is known, what is measured, and what is still dark.

  • 19
    The Milky Way From Inside

    Explain why the galaxy looks like a band, say where we sit in it, and give the scale of it in time as well as distance.

  • 20
    Galaxies and the Great Rush

    Classify a galaxy by shape and explain expansion without putting a centre anywhere, including here.

  • 21
    The Beginning and the Dark

    Say what the leftover glow is and why it counts as evidence, and state plainly what dark matter and dark energy are and are not.

6. Getting There

How you actually leave, where you can go, and what it takes to stay alive once you have. Numbers, budgets and trade-offs.

  • 22
    How Rockets Work

    Explain thrust with nothing to push against, and say from the numbers why a rocket is almost entirely fuel and has to be thrown away in stages.

  • 23
    Up, and Back Down

    Explain why going to space is mostly sideways, and why coming back is hot for a reason that is not friction.

  • 24
    Going Somewhere Else

    Plan a transfer to Mars, say why the window comes round every 26 months, and use a planet to steal speed.

  • 25
    Staying Alive Out There

    List what a spacesuit and a spacecraft must each do, and say which of them is hardest for a three-year trip.

7. People, Probes and Questions

How this was all worked out, mostly by people with worse equipment than a phone, and the question nobody has answered.

  • 26
    How We Worked It Out

    Measure the Earth with a stick and a shadow, and give the evidence that settled the argument about what goes round what.

  • 27
    The Space Age

    Put the first sixty years of spaceflight in order and say what was driving each stretch of it.

  • 28
    Are We Alone?

    Find a planet by watching a star dim, define a habitable zone, and use the Drake equation honestly rather than to get an answer they like.

8. Capstone

Design something, observe something, and present both.

  • 29
    Design a Mission

    Write a one-page mission proposal: destination, question, instruments, mass budget and launch window, all defensible.

  • 30
    Observation Night

    Log a real night's observing and present what they saw, what they expected, and what did not match.

1 of 30 lessons written. No accounts, no analytics, nothing tracked. Open any file in a browser — there is nothing to build. The computers course is next door.
